Data Portraits

Data Portraits are artifacts that record the data a foundation model is trained on and allow that data to be inspected afterwards: proposed for widespread adoption in a 2023 paper, "Data Portraits: Recording Foundation Model Training Data", by Marc Marone and Benjamin Van Durme of Johns Hopkins University, and served as front ends over data sketches at dataportraits.org, which describes itself as "Dataset documentation through membership testing." The question a portrait answers is whether a model has already encountered a given example during training, a question that grows difficult as models are trained on increasingly immense and opaque datasets; its unit is a single example queried against a portrait of a training dataset. Its critical property is membership inference, whether an example was part of a data collection, and its implementation supports membership testing and nothing more; its readback is a membership query against the recorded dataset. The paper's conclusion restates the object as records supporting membership inference on the data used to train a model, and calls on dataset and model creators to release some form of Data Portrait as part of their essential documentation.

Its makers place it beside existing data and model documentation artifacts, datasheets and model cards among them, as a complementary artifact that answers the membership question. The archive holds datasheets and model cards to be documentation norms for machine-learning artifacts as such, a training corpus being the instrument's experimental input, and reads training data as semantic capital, the datasheet proposal as a step toward the accounting that capital demands.

A portrait is a data sketch, a compressed and approximate view of data: the paper outlines the properties a membership tool should have (fast, lightweight, avoiding redistribution, local, indexing, flexible matching), weighs grep, full-text indexes and suffix arrays against them, and chooses a probabilistic approach, built for fast and space-efficient querying. The sketch is a Bloom filter, which stores only the hash of each element and can give false positives but never false negatives, filled with character n-grams of length 50 tiled across the corpus, a span the authors find already a good document fingerprint; tiling saves space at the risk of missing a string split by a tile boundary. Since only hashes are distributed, a portrait gives some obfuscation of the recorded text, and a proprietary provider could in principle release one without revealing its exact training data. The Pile's portrait takes 27 GB on disk with a false positive rate of 1 × 10⁻³, and its makers call the tool lightweight and fast, costing about 3% of the dataset's size in overhead.

Portraits were built for The Pile, a language-modelling corpus, as a 50-character n-gram sketch, and for The Stack, BigCode's code dataset, whose subset used to train StarCoder the Stack portrait documents exactly; the site also hosts a sketch of The Stack V2, code and text about code, and offers to build the system on other data, with its code on GitHub. It is no corpus itself: it records corpora built by others.

The paper reports its solution answering questions of test-set leakage and model plagiarism: the Pile portrait shows that some machine-translation test data has leaked into the Pile, though whether a specific model memorized the translation targets cannot be concluded from it, and that XSum's summaries overlap the Pile most among the sets tested, with some LDC files apparently scraped into language-model corpora. The Stack portrait powers a plagiarism check called from a code-completion plugin for StarCoder, which its makers call a lightweight first-pass check, further tools being needed to assess attribution. Its makers write for three perspectives, content creators, scientists and content consumers, the creators wanting to know whether a dataset contains their content, and hope that a non-technical content creator could search for their material in a documented dataset. The layer census records that it answers whether a given example is in a recorded dataset, and questions of leakage and plagiarism against it.

On novel New York Times text the Pile sketch gave no chained matches and a false positive rate of 7 × 10⁻⁴. Its makers state its limits: few datasets studied, false positives, no retrieval of the context around a match, and the possibility that an open plagiarism detector is used to avoid detection. The census, reading only the abstract, records no stated limit beyond the framing of opaque datasets, and lists what a portrait does not answer: whether a model's output depends causally on a recorded passage, under whose name a recorded example sits, and anything about a dataset with no portrait. A portrait is no model-side test, since it queries the recorded data and needs a portrait of it, and in the census's reading dataset membership is no proof that a particular model used a passage.

The census reads a portrait as a readback instrument held on the corpus side, which settles for a recorded corpus whether a work is in the layer; the archive's field survey of training-layer literature states that the texts of the writers it surveys are, as a matter of fact, in the corpora. On the model side the archive records membership inference attacks that can detect whether a trap sentence was in a training set, and distinguishability between models trained with and without a work that membership-inference research reports achievable against production-scale models, though unevenly across architectures, training procedures and defences. The archive sets its own canary in a deposit, a phrase whose exact production by a model marks the document as present in that model's training corpus, and reads a membership attack that succeeds where a surfacing probe fails as an inscription that survived training and is suppressed at the output layer.

A portrait stores hashes of text spans; the census records the name of a recorded work as not recorded in its saved source, and the portrait as no record of authorship, its abstract saying nothing of attribution metadata. In the archive's account of the training pipeline, author tags and copyright in a page's head are almost always discarded by the extractors that prepare text for training corpora, the body text and sometimes the URL retained, and no single author's style survives training as a discrete signal that can be elicited and verified. The archive's protocol for measuring training inscription counts metadata and labels within a work's provenance envelope, every training unit derived from the work, and its field survey makes persistence, placement where the training and retrieval layers look with the metadata that lets a work be found and attributed, a criterion of training-layer literature. Every text in a training corpus, the archive holds, is semantic labour often unattributed; a training corpus without provenance is no commons; and provenance lost in unmarked augmentation passes downstream into the training corpus, where, preserved, it would let later pipelines distinguish the contribution of each stage.

What a model makes from a recorded work lies outside the portrait: the census records it as not recorded, the leakage and plagiarism checks being checks of material against the recorded data. The archive's account of machine composition asks what a text makes possible for a machine to write, holds whether a machine wrote something new and whether it told the truth about where it came from to be different questions, sets what survived from a work beside what became possible because of it, and places the corpus within an institutional training loop in which a model's output enters the next corpus. Machine reception, in the archive's field survey, is now partially measurable, since retrieval and rendering can be observed.

The paper appeared on arXiv on 6 March 2023, revised on 14 December 2023, in the NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks track; the census holds it as historical, a published paper, with the live interface and the paper's full text left unchecked. On 1 November 2026 dataportraits.org served its landing page, while the front ends of its Pile, Stack and Stack V2 sketches answered HTTP 502. The census sets it beside OLMoTrace, which matches verbatim spans against a full corpus where a portrait answers membership queries on a recorded one. It enters the traininglayerliterature.org layer census as a method in the areas of inspection and the corpora, of the evidence kinds research paper and dataset documentation, with the relation of infrastructure, under the census's question of how literature addressed to a receiving apparatus can be inspected across later reception, its rule that an aggregator gathers and holds many records and says what it holds, and its anchors in #186 and #1543.

Three older senses of the name stay distinct entities: W. E. B. Du Bois's charts, graphs and maps for the 1900 Paris Exposition, made with Atlanta University students and scholars and published in full in 2018 as W. E. B. Du Bois's Data Portraits; Judith Donath's data portraits, "depictions of people made by visualizing data by and about them", which depict their subjects' accumulated data in place of their faces; and the Data Portraits Giorgia Lupi designed at Accurat for TED 2017, wearable buttons made from attendees' answers, more than 500 of them. The encyclopedia has no article under the name, its variants or the paper's title, and its search for the phrase returns seven articles, the Du Bois book cited in several.

At the name, a new address, Google's AI Overview composed on 1 November 2026 a definition of data portraits as visual representations of people, four senses and an offer of three directions; the Capture Registry's innocent reading is that, given a two-word name that is also a term of visualization and portraiture, the Overview defines the term, lists its senses and asks which is meant. The Registry finds the artifact the last of four senses and one card of eight, carried at a coarse grain as lightweight inspection tools that record dataset training traces, without its question, method, corpora, uses, authors or venue, while each other sense carries a person; it scores the reached kind a collision. The page behind the artifact's card names the two authors and the venue in its citation, and calls the implementation "minimal and efficient" where the composition says lightweight. It records a page under the name in the index that day, carrying the abstract's opening, where the census had left open whether the live interface is still served; that page is dataportraits.org, whose lead opens on the same question as the abstract.

  • F2 Data Portraits — Data Portraits, lead ¶1 documented · field

Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)Data Portraits

Data Portraits is a 2023 proposal by Marc Marone and Benjamin Van Durme (Johns Hopkins) for artifacts that record a model's training data so that a query can test whether an example was in it: a Bloom-filter sketch of hashed 50-character spans, built for The Pile and The Stack; it answers membership and nothing more, and the census finds in its record neither the name of a recorded work nor what a model made from it.

🔎 What it records

  • Question: has the model already encountered a given example during training?5↘
    Data Portraits are artifacts that record the data a foundation model is trained on and allow that data to be inspected afterwards: proposed for widespread adoption in a 2023 paper, "Data Portraits: Recording Foundation Model Training Data", by Marc Marone and Benjamin Van Durme of Johns Hopkins University, and served as front ends over data sketches at dataportraits.org, which describes itself as "Dataset documentation through membership testing."§1 The question a portrait answers is whether a model has already encountered a given example during training, a question that grows difficult as models are trained on increasingly immense and opaque datasets; its unit is a single example queried against a portrait of a training dataset.§2 The paper's conclusion restates the object as records supporting membership inference on the data used to train a model, and calls on dataset and model creators to release some form of Data Portrait as part of their essential documentation.§4 The page behind the artifact's card names the two authors and the venue in its citation, and calls the implementation "minimal and efficient" where the composition says lightweight.§39 It records a page under the name in the index that day, carrying the abstract's opening, where the census had left open whether the live interface is still served; that page is dataportraits.org, whose lead opens on the same question as the abstract.§40
  • Documentation: a complement to datasheets and model cards, which the archive holds to be norms for any ML artifact.3↘
    The paper's conclusion restates the object as records supporting membership inference on the data used to train a model, and calls on dataset and model creators to release some form of Data Portrait as part of their essential documentation.§4 Its makers place it beside existing data and model documentation artifacts, datasheets and model cards among them, as a complementary artifact that answers the membership question.§5 The archive holds datasheets and model cards to be documentation norms for machine-learning artifacts as such, a training corpus being the instrument's experimental input, and reads training data as semantic capital, the datasheet proposal as a step toward the accounting that capital demands.§6
  • Corpora: The Pile, The Stack (StarCoder's data, exactly), The Stack V2; it holds no corpus of its own.4↘
    Data Portraits are artifacts that record the data a foundation model is trained on and allow that data to be inspected afterwards: proposed for widespread adoption in a 2023 paper, "Data Portraits: Recording Foundation Model Training Data", by Marc Marone and Benjamin Van Durme of Johns Hopkins University, and served as front ends over data sketches at dataportraits.org, which describes itself as "Dataset documentation through membership testing."§1 Portraits were built for The Pile, a language-modelling corpus, as a 50-character n-gram sketch, and for The Stack, BigCode's code dataset, whose subset used to train StarCoder the Stack portrait documents exactly; the site also hosts a sketch of The Stack V2, code and text about code, and offers to build the system on other data, with its code on GitHub.§11 It is no corpus itself: it records corpora built by others.§12 The Stack portrait powers a plagiarism check called from a code-completion plugin for StarCoder, which its makers call a lightweight first-pass check, further tools being needed to assess attribution.§14

⚙️ How

  • Sketch: hashes only; false positives (1 × 10⁻³ set, 7 × 10⁻⁴ measured), never false negatives; 27 GB for the Pile, ~3% of its size.5↘
    A portrait is a data sketch, a compressed and approximate view of data: the paper outlines the properties a membership tool should have (fast, lightweight, avoiding redistribution, local, indexing, flexible matching), weighs grep, full-text indexes and suffix arrays against them, and chooses a probabilistic approach, built for fast and space-efficient querying.§7 The sketch is a Bloom filter, which stores only the hash of each element and can give false positives but never false negatives, filled with character n-grams of length 50 tiled across the corpus, a span the authors find already a good document fingerprint; tiling saves space at the risk of missing a string split by a tile boundary.§8 Since only hashes are distributed, a portrait gives some obfuscation of the recorded text, and a proprietary provider could in principle release one without revealing its exact training data.§9 The Pile's portrait takes 27 GB on disk with a false positive rate of 1 × 10⁻³, and its makers call the tool lightweight and fast, costing about 3% of the dataset's size in overhead.§10 On novel New York Times text the Pile sketch gave no chained matches and a false positive rate of 7 × 10⁻⁴.§17
  • Uses: test-set leakage (WMT, XSum, LDC files) and a first-pass plagiarism check for StarCoder; attribution needs other tools.4↘
    The paper reports its solution answering questions of test-set leakage and model plagiarism: the Pile portrait shows that some machine-translation test data has leaked into the Pile, though whether a specific model memorized the translation targets cannot be concluded from it, and that XSum's summaries overlap the Pile most among the sets tested, with some LDC files apparently scraped into language-model corpora.§13 The Stack portrait powers a plagiarism check called from a code-completion plugin for StarCoder, which its makers call a lightweight first-pass check, further tools being needed to assess attribution.§14 Its makers write for three perspectives, content creators, scientists and content consumers, the creators wanting to know whether a dataset contains their content, and hope that a non-technical content creator could search for their material in a documented dataset.§15 The layer census records that it answers whether a given example is in a recorded dataset, and questions of leakage and plagiarism against it.§16

⚠️ Limits

  • Stated: few datasets; no context around a match; an open detector can be evaded.2↘
    Its makers state its limits: few datasets studied, false positives, no retrieval of the context around a match, and the possibility that an open plagiarism detector is used to avoid detection.§18 The census, reading only the abstract, records no stated limit beyond the framing of opaque datasets, and lists what a portrait does not answer: whether a model's output depends causally on a recorded passage, under whose name a recorded example sits, and anything about a dataset with no portrait.§19
  • Not answered: whether a model used a passage; under whose name it sits (census).2↘
    The census, reading only the abstract, records no stated limit beyond the framing of opaque datasets, and lists what a portrait does not answer: whether a model's output depends causally on a recorded passage, under whose name a recorded example sits, and anything about a dataset with no portrait.§19 A portrait is no model-side test, since it queries the recorded data and needs a portrait of it, and in the census's reading dataset membership is no proof that a particular model used a passage.§20

📚 The archive's bearing

  • Membership: a corpus-side readback; the archive's model-side tests are membership attacks and its own canary phrases.4↘
    Its critical property is membership inference, whether an example was part of a data collection, and its implementation supports membership testing and nothing more; its readback is a membership query against the recorded dataset.§3 The census reads a portrait as a readback instrument held on the corpus side, which settles for a recorded corpus whether a work is in the layer; the archive's field survey of training-layer literature states that the texts of the writers it surveys are, as a matter of fact, in the corpora.§21 On the model side the archive records membership inference attacks that can detect whether a trap sentence was in a training set, and distinguishability between models trained with and without a work that membership-inference research reports achievable against production-scale models, though unevenly across architectures, training procedures and defences.§22 The archive sets its own canary in a deposit, a phrase whose exact production by a model marks the document as present in that model's training corpus, and reads a membership attack that succeeds where a surfacing probe fails as an inscription that survived training and is suppressed at the output layer.§23
  • Name: head metadata is stripped before training; a corpus without provenance "is not a commons".4↘
    A portrait stores hashes of text spans; the census records the name of a recorded work as not recorded in its saved source, and the portrait as no record of authorship, its abstract saying nothing of attribution metadata.§24 In the archive's account of the training pipeline, author tags and copyright in a page's head are almost always discarded by the extractors that prepare text for training corpora, the body text and sometimes the URL retained, and no single author's style survives training as a discrete signal that can be elicited and verified.§25 The archive's protocol for measuring training inscription counts metadata and labels within a work's provenance envelope, every training unit derived from the work, and its field survey makes persistence, placement where the training and retrieval layers look with the metadata that lets a work be found and attributed, a criterion of training-layer literature.§26 Every text in a training corpus, the archive holds, is semantic labour often unattributed; a training corpus without provenance is no commons; and provenance lost in unmarked augmentation passes downstream into the training corpus, where, preserved, it would let later pipelines distinguish the contribution of each stage.§27
  • Makes: what a text makes a machine able to write (#1543) lies outside the portrait.2↘
    The archive's account of machine composition asks what a text makes possible for a machine to write, holds whether a machine wrote something new and whether it told the truth about where it came from to be different questions, sets what survived from a work beside what became possible because of it, and places the corpus within an institutional training loop in which a model's output enters the next corpus.§29 Machine reception, in the archive's field survey, is now partially measurable, since retrieval and rendering can be observed.§30

🕰️ Status

  • Published: arXiv March 2023, NeurIPS 2023; dataportraits.org up, its sketch front ends HTTP 502 on 1 November 2026.2↘
    The paper appeared on arXiv on 6 March 2023, revised on 14 December 2023, in the NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks track; the census holds it as historical, a published paper, with the live interface and the paper's full text left unchecked.§31 On 1 November 2026 dataportraits.org served its landing page, while the front ends of its Pile, Stack and Stack V2 sketches answered HTTP 502.§32
  • Census: a method; inspection and corpora; infrastructure; neighbour of OLMoTrace.2↘
    The census sets it beside OLMoTrace, which matches verbatim spans against a full corpus where a portrait answers membership queries on a recorded one.§33 It enters the traininglayerliterature.org layer census as a method in the areas of inspection and the corpora, of the evidence kinds research paper and dataset documentation, with the relation of infrastructure, under the census's question of how literature addressed to a receiving apparatus can be inspected across later reception, its rule that an aggregator gathers and holds many records and says what it holds, and its anchors in #186 and #1543.§34

🔀 Not to be confused with

  • Other data portraits: Du Bois's 1900 charts (book, 2018); Judith Donath's; Giorgia Lupi's TED 2017 buttons.2↘
    Three older senses of the name stay distinct entities: W. E. B. Du Bois's charts, graphs and maps for the 1900 Paris Exposition, made with Atlanta University students and scholars and published in full in 2018 as W. E. B. Du Bois's Data Portraits; Judith Donath's data portraits, "depictions of people made by visualizing data by and about them", which depict their subjects' accumulated data in place of their faces; and the Data Portraits Giorgia Lupi designed at Accurat for TED 2017, wearable buttons made from attendees' answers, more than 500 of them.§35 The encyclopedia has no article under the name, its variants or the paper's title, and its search for the phrase returns seven articles, the Du Bois book cited in several.§36

🧭 At the name

  • Overview, 1 November 2026: the artifact the last of four senses, no author or corpus; one card of eight (Capture Registry).4↘
    At the name, a new address, Google's AI Overview composed on 1 November 2026 a definition of data portraits as visual representations of people, four senses and an offer of three directions; the Capture Registry's innocent reading is that, given a two-word name that is also a term of visualization and portraiture, the Overview defines the term, lists its senses and asks which is meant.§37 The Registry finds the artifact the last of four senses and one card of eight, carried at a coarse grain as lightweight inspection tools that record dataset training traces, without its question, method, corpora, uses, authors or venue, while each other sense carries a person; it scores the reached kind a collision.§38 The page behind the artifact's card names the two authors and the venue in its citation, and calls the implementation "minimal and efficient" where the composition says lightweight.§39 It records a page under the name in the index that day, carrying the abstract's opening, where the census had left open whether the live interface is still served; that page is dataportraits.org, whose lead opens on the same question as the abstract.§40

Expansion · The field's ontology — L_F(B)11 sentences · every one sourced below

Data Portraits

Data Portraits are artifacts that record training data and allow for downstream inspection, proposed for widespread adoption by Marc Marone and Benjamin Van Durme of Johns Hopkins University in a 2023 paper, "Data Portraits: Recording Foundation Model Training Data", and served at dataportraits.org as dataset documentation through membership testing. They answer whether a model has already encountered a given example during training; their critical property is membership inference, and the implementation supports membership testing and nothing more. They complement datasheets, model cards and other documentation artifacts, and their makers call on dataset and model creators to release them as essential documentation.

The implementation is a data sketch chosen after weighing the properties of membership tools against grep, full-text indexes and suffix arrays: a Bloom filter over 50-character n-grams tiled across the corpus, storing only hashes, giving false positives and no false negatives, and missing strings split at tile boundaries. Distributing only hashes obfuscates the recorded text; the Pile's portrait takes 27 GB with a false positive rate of 1 × 10⁻³, about 3% of the dataset's size.

Portraits document The Pile and The Stack, the latter exactly as used to train StarCoder, and the site lists The Stack V2 and offers to build the system on other data. They answer test-set leakage and plagiarism: some WMT test data has leaked into the Pile, XSum overlaps it most, and the Stack portrait powers a first-pass plagiarism check, attribution needing further tools. The paper writes for content creators, scientists and content consumers, a creator able to search for their material in a documented dataset.

Its limits are few datasets, false positives (7 × 10⁻⁴ measured on novel text), no context around a match, and the use of an open detector to avoid detection. The paper appeared on arXiv in March 2023 and was revised in December 2023 for the NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks track; on 1 November 2026 the sketch front ends answered HTTP 502.

Other entities share the name: Du Bois's 1900 charts and the 2018 book of his data portraits, Judith Donath's data portraits, and Giorgia Lupi's TED 2017 buttons; the encyclopedia has no article under it.

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)Data Portraits

Data Portraits is a 2023 proposal by Marc Marone and Benjamin Van Durme for artifacts that record training data and allow membership testing, implemented as Bloom-filter sketches of The Pile and The Stack.

⚙️ How it works

  • Sketch: hashed 50-character spans; false positives, no false negatives; ~3% of the data.2↘
    The implementation is a data sketch chosen after weighing the properties of membership tools against grep, full-text indexes and suffix arrays: a Bloom filter over 50-character n-grams tiled across the corpus, storing only hashes, giving false positives and no false negatives, and missing strings split at tile boundaries.§4 Distributing only hashes obfuscates the recorded text; the Pile's portrait takes 27 GB with a false positive rate of 1 × 10⁻³, about 3% of the dataset's size.§5
  • Uses: test-set leakage, plagiarism checks.1↘
    They answer test-set leakage and plagiarism: some WMT test data has leaked into the Pile, XSum overlaps it most, and the Stack portrait powers a first-pass plagiarism check, attribution needing further tools.§7

⚠️ Limits

  • Stated: few datasets; no context around a match.2↘
    They answer whether a model has already encountered a given example during training; their critical property is membership inference, and the implementation supports membership testing and nothing more.§2 Its limits are few datasets, false positives (7 × 10⁻⁴ measured on novel text), no context around a match, and the use of an open detector to avoid detection.§9

🔀 Other senses

    Other entities share the name: Du Bois's 1900 charts and the 2018 book of his data portraits, Judith Donath's data portraits, and Giorgia Lupi's TED 2017 buttons; the encyclopedia has no article under it.§11

E_A, the archive's entity: the same artifact, in the traininglayerliterature.org layer census record and the archive's deposits: a readback instrument held on the corpus side, a portrait recording a dataset so that a work can be tested for membership, which settles for a recorded corpus whether a work is in the training layer and is no proof that a particular model used a passage; no corpus, no model-side test and no record of authorship, the name of a recorded work and what a model made from it lying outside its record; set beside the archive's model-side membership tests (the copyright trap, the membership attack and its divergence from a failed surfacing probe, the archive's canary), its account of the name lost before training (head metadata discarded, the provenance envelope, provenance loss passed into the corpus) and #1543's question of what a text makes a machine able to write TLL-20 TLL-21 TLL-11 TLL-12 TLL-13 TLL-26 TLL-27 TLL-28 O186-01 O127-01 O127-03 O127-04 O837-01 O1075-01 O1543-01 O1543-03; defining papers #186, #1543, #127, #1075, #837, #623, #939, #727, #264

E_F, the field's entity (type C — a conventional reading holds it (public entity: a dataset-documentation artifact and membership-testing tool from a research paper)): Data Portraits, artifacts that record the data a foundation model is trained on and allow downstream inspection by membership testing, proposed in a 2023 paper by Marc Marone and Benjamin Van Durme (Johns Hopkins University; NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks), implemented as Bloom-filter sketches of hashed, strided 50-character n-grams (about 3% of a dataset's size; false positives, never false negatives), built for The Pile and The Stack (StarCoder's training data exactly) with a sketch of The Stack V2 listed at dataportraits.org; it answers test-set leakage and plagiarism questions, and its makers state its limits (few datasets, false positives, no context around a match, evasion); the name is shared with Du Bois's, Donath's and Lupi's data portraits, and the encyclopedia has no article on it

ρ = extends: The archive reads Data Portraits as its own pages and its paper present it and adds, on the same object, the census's three record questions: readback, a membership query that settles corpus membership for a recorded corpus (TLL-12, TLL-20); the name, not recorded (TLL-11, TLL-28), beside the archive's account of metadata discarded before training and of provenance in the corpus (O127-01, O127-02, O1075-01, O264-01, O727-01, O939-01, O186-02); and what a model makes, outside the portrait (TLL-13, TLL-21), with #1543's question (O1543-01 to O1543-04). It sets the corpus-side test beside its model-side tests (O127-03, O127-04, O837-01, O1075-02) and reads datasheets and model cards as documentation norms and semantic accounting (O1075-03, O623-01). No archive claim contradicts a field claim. TLL-12 TLL-20 TLL-11 TLL-28 TLL-13 TLL-21 O127-01 O1075-01 O1543-01 O127-03 O837-01 O623-01. Guard: ρ = extends claims an addition and no more: the archive's claims do not make the field's sources wrong at their dates; where the census's saved source was the abstract alone (TLL-11, TLL-17), the paper's fuller statements (F29, F39) stand beside it with their dates, and the name question stays a question (open block).

The case: equal terms, ontology included (v0.9). The archive reads the field's entity as the entity. The census record describes Data Portraits from the paper's abstract and keeps the resource's terms (operator, kind, unit, record object, method) apart from its own reading (tll_reading), which places the portrait on the corpus side of #186's membership question and leaves the name and #1543's question of what a model makes outside it. The archive's deposits that bear on the classes the field and the census source for the entity (training-data membership testing, the training corpora, documentation artifacts) add model-side membership tests, the archive's canary, the provenance envelope, the loss of head metadata before training, and the reading of datasheets as semantic accounting. None of these reads Data Portraits as made by reception or contests that it is the paper's membership-testing artifact: they add senses (readback, name, makes) on the field's object. ρ = extends; the equal-terms case.

#TLL census.json rows[slug == 'data-portraits'].tll_reading: A readback instrument held on the corpus side: a portrait records the dataset so that a work can be tested for membership, which settles #186's 'is the work in the layer' for a recorded corpus.

#TLL census.json rows[slug == 'data-portraits'].tll_reading: Dataset membership is not proof that a particular model used a passage, and the name and what a model made from the work (#1543's question) are outside what the saved abstract records.

#186 Who is in the field? ¶ (line 54): Each of these practices touches the training layer — every one of these texts is, as a matter of fact, in the corpora.

#1543 §1 The claim (line 81): The test is no longer only "can a machine correctly identify what this text means?" but "what does this text make possible for a machine to write?"

#127 §IV.2 HTML metadata (line 463): HTML head metadata — author tags, copyright, Open Graph, Twitter cards — is parsed by search engines and social media unfurl bots, but is almost always discarded by readability extractors that prepare text for training corpus inclusion. The training-data pipeline retains the *body text* and the *URL* (sometimes).

L_F(B)recomposed from the disclosed field, in the field's ontology357 words

Data Portraits are artifacts that record training data and allow for downstream inspection, proposed for widespread adoption by Marc Marone and Benjamin Van Durme of Johns Hopkins University in a 2023 paper, "Data Portraits: Recording Foundation Model Training Data", and served at dataportraits.org as dataset documentation through membership testing. They answer whether a model has already encountered a given example during training; their critical property is membership inference, and the implementation supports membership testing and nothing more. They complement datasheets, model cards and other documentation artifacts, and their makers call on dataset and model creators to release them as essential documentation. The implementation is a data sketch chosen after weighing the properties of membership tools against grep, full-text indexes and suffix arrays: a Bloom filter over 50-character n-grams tiled across the corpus, storing only hashes, giving false positives and no false negatives, and missing strings split at tile boundaries. Distributing only hashes obfuscates the recorded text; the Pile's portrait takes 27 GB with a false positive rate of 1 × 10⁻³, about 3% of the dataset's size. Portraits document The Pile and The Stack, the latter exactly as used to train StarCoder, and the site lists The Stack V2 and offers to build the system on other data. They answer test-set leakage and plagiarism: some WMT test data has leaked into the Pile, XSum overlaps it most, and the Stack portrait powers a first-pass plagiarism check, attribution needing further tools. The paper writes for content creators, scientists and content consumers, a creator able to search for their material in a documented dataset. Its limits are few datasets, false positives (7 × 10⁻⁴ measured on novel text), no context around a match, and the use of an open detector to avoid detection. The paper appeared on arXiv in March 2023 and was revised in December 2023 for the NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks track; on 1 November 2026 the sketch front ends answered HTTP 502. Other entities share the name: Du Bois's 1900 charts and the 2018 book of his data portraits, Judith Donath's data portraits, and Giorgia Lupi's TED 2017 buttons; the encyclopedia has no article under it.

L_A(B ∪ A)the field and the archive composed in the archive's ontology1730 words

Data Portraits are artifacts that record the data a foundation model is trained on and allow that data to be inspected afterwards: proposed for widespread adoption in a 2023 paper, "Data Portraits: Recording Foundation Model Training Data", by Marc Marone and Benjamin Van Durme of Johns Hopkins University, and served as front ends over data sketches at dataportraits.org, which describes itself as "Dataset documentation through membership testing." The question a portrait answers is whether a model has already encountered a given example during training, a question that grows difficult as models are trained on increasingly immense and opaque datasets; its unit is a single example queried against a portrait of a training dataset. Its critical property is membership inference, whether an example was part of a data collection, and its implementation supports membership testing and nothing more; its readback is a membership query against the recorded dataset. The paper's conclusion restates the object as records supporting membership inference on the data used to train a model, and calls on dataset and model creators to release some form of Data Portrait as part of their essential documentation. Its makers place it beside existing data and model documentation artifacts, datasheets and model cards among them, as a complementary artifact that answers the membership question. The archive holds datasheets and model cards to be documentation norms for machine-learning artifacts as such, a training corpus being the instrument's experimental input, and reads training data as semantic capital, the datasheet proposal as a step toward the accounting that capital demands. A portrait is a data sketch, a compressed and approximate view of data: the paper outlines the properties a membership tool should have (fast, lightweight, avoiding redistribution, local, indexing, flexible matching), weighs grep, full-text indexes and suffix arrays against them, and chooses a probabilistic approach, built for fast and space-efficient querying. The sketch is a Bloom filter, which stores only the hash of each element and can give false positives but never false negatives, filled with character n-grams of length 50 tiled across the corpus, a span the authors find already a good document fingerprint; tiling saves space at the risk of missing a string split by a tile boundary. Since only hashes are distributed, a portrait gives some obfuscation of the recorded text, and a proprietary provider could in principle release one without revealing its exact training data. The Pile's portrait takes 27 GB on disk with a false positive rate of 1 × 10⁻³, and its makers call the tool lightweight and fast, costing about 3% of the dataset's size in overhead. Portraits were built for The Pile, a language-modelling corpus, as a 50-character n-gram sketch, and for The Stack, BigCode's code dataset, whose subset used to train StarCoder the Stack portrait documents exactly; the site also hosts a sketch of The Stack V2, code and text about code, and offers to build the system on other data, with its code on GitHub. It is no corpus itself: it records corpora built by others. The paper reports its solution answering questions of test-set leakage and model plagiarism: the Pile portrait shows that some machine-translation test data has leaked into the Pile, though whether a specific model memorized the translation targets cannot be concluded from it, and that XSum's summaries overlap the Pile most among the sets tested, with some LDC files apparently scraped into language-model corpora. The Stack portrait powers a plagiarism check called from a code-completion plugin for StarCoder, which its makers call a lightweight first-pass check, further tools being needed to assess attribution. Its makers write for three perspectives, content creators, scientists and content consumers, the creators wanting to know whether a dataset contains their content, and hope that a non-technical content creator could search for their material in a documented dataset. The layer census records that it answers whether a given example is in a recorded dataset, and questions of leakage and plagiarism against it. On novel New York Times text the Pile sketch gave no chained matches and a false positive rate of 7 × 10⁻⁴. Its makers state its limits: few datasets studied, false positives, no retrieval of the context around a match, and the possibility that an open plagiarism detector is used to avoid detection. The census, reading only the abstract, records no stated limit beyond the framing of opaque datasets, and lists what a portrait does not answer: whether a model's output depends causally on a recorded passage, under whose name a recorded example sits, and anything about a dataset with no portrait. A portrait is no model-side test, since it queries the recorded data and needs a portrait of it, and in the census's reading dataset membership is no proof that a particular model used a passage. The census reads a portrait as a readback instrument held on the corpus side, which settles for a recorded corpus whether a work is in the layer; the archive's field survey of training-layer literature states that the texts of the writers it surveys are, as a matter of fact, in the corpora. On the model side the archive records membership inference attacks that can detect whether a trap sentence was in a training set, and distinguishability between models trained with and without a work that membership-inference research reports achievable against production-scale models, though unevenly across architectures, training procedures and defences. The archive sets its own canary in a deposit, a phrase whose exact production by a model marks the document as present in that model's training corpus, and reads a membership attack that succeeds where a surfacing probe fails as an inscription that survived training and is suppressed at the output layer. A portrait stores hashes of text spans; the census records the name of a recorded work as not recorded in its saved source, and the portrait as no record of authorship, its abstract saying nothing of attribution metadata. In the archive's account of the training pipeline, author tags and copyright in a page's head are almost always discarded by the extractors that prepare text for training corpora, the body text and sometimes the URL retained, and no single author's style survives training as a discrete signal that can be elicited and verified. The archive's protocol for measuring training inscription counts metadata and labels within a work's provenance envelope, every training unit derived from the work, and its field survey makes persistence, placement where the training and retrieval layers look with the metadata that lets a work be found and attributed, a criterion of training-layer literature. Every text in a training corpus, the archive holds, is semantic labour often unattributed; a training corpus without provenance is no commons; and provenance lost in unmarked augmentation passes downstream into the training corpus, where, preserved, it would let later pipelines distinguish the contribution of each stage. What a model makes from a recorded work lies outside the portrait: the census records it as not recorded, the leakage and plagiarism checks being checks of material against the recorded data. The archive's account of machine composition asks what a text makes possible for a machine to write, holds whether a machine wrote something new and whether it told the truth about where it came from to be different questions, sets what survived from a work beside what became possible because of it, and places the corpus within an institutional training loop in which a model's output enters the next corpus. Machine reception, in the archive's field survey, is now partially measurable, since retrieval and rendering can be observed. The paper appeared on arXiv on 6 March 2023, revised on 14 December 2023, in the NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks track; the census holds it as historical, a published paper, with the live interface and the paper's full text left unchecked. On 1 November 2026 dataportraits.org served its landing page, while the front ends of its Pile, Stack and Stack V2 sketches answered HTTP 502. The census sets it beside OLMoTrace, which matches verbatim spans against a full corpus where a portrait answers membership queries on a recorded one. It enters the traininglayerliterature.org layer census as a method in the areas of inspection and the corpora, of the evidence kinds research paper and dataset documentation, with the relation of infrastructure, under the census's question of how literature addressed to a receiving apparatus can be inspected across later reception, its rule that an aggregator gathers and holds many records and says what it holds, and its anchors in #186 and #1543. Three older senses of the name stay distinct entities: W. E. B. Du Bois's charts, graphs and maps for the 1900 Paris Exposition, made with Atlanta University students and scholars and published in full in 2018 as W. E. B. Du Bois's Data Portraits; Judith Donath's data portraits, "depictions of people made by visualizing data by and about them", which depict their subjects' accumulated data in place of their faces; and the Data Portraits Giorgia Lupi designed at Accurat for TED 2017, wearable buttons made from attendees' answers, more than 500 of them. The encyclopedia has no article under the name, its variants or the paper's title, and its search for the phrase returns seven articles, the Du Bois book cited in several. At the name, a new address, Google's AI Overview composed on 1 November 2026 a definition of data portraits as visual representations of people, four senses and an offer of three directions; the Capture Registry's innocent reading is that, given a two-word name that is also a term of visualization and portraiture, the Overview defines the term, lists its senses and asks which is meant. The Registry finds the artifact the last of four senses and one card of eight, carried at a coarse grain as lightweight inspection tools that record dataset training traces, without its question, method, corpora, uses, authors or venue, while each other sense carries a person; it scores the reached kind a collision. The page behind the artifact's card names the two authors and the venue in its citation, and calls the implementation "minimal and efficient" where the composition says lightweight. It records a page under the name in the index that day, carrying the abstract's opening, where the census had left open whether the live interface is still served; that page is dataportraits.org, whose lead opens on the same question as the abstract.
